en: Annotated by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Mount Guifeng at the Aranya;
this is an annotation on the *Huayan fajie guanmen*,
cultivated through the practice and realization of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* is the foundational scripture.
"Great, Vast, and Extensive" (*Mahāvaipulya*) refers to the Dharma that is realized;
"Buddha-Flower-Adornment" (*Buddhāvataṃsaka*) refers to the person who realizes it.
"Great" refers to the essence—
the essential nature of the minds of all Buddhas and sentient beings.
"Vast and Broad" refers to the characteristics and functions of that very essence.
The Buddha represents the fruit;
the Avataṃsaka Sūtra represents the cause.
The flowers serve as a metaphor for the myriad practices.
Austerity is itself great wisdom;
with great wisdom as its sovereign,
it directs the myriad practices.
"Adorning the Vaipulya" refers to the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood;
it omits the character "sūtra."
The meaning does not reside in the literal text.
*Fajie qingliang xing jingshu* (Commentary on the New Sutra of the Pure and Cool Dharma Realm) states:
"It comprehensively unifies the single True Dharma Realm."
This means that, encompassing all phenomena in their entirety,
they are none other than the single mind;
yet, this mind permeates and integrates all phenomena.
Thus, four kinds of dharma-dhātus are established.
First is the dharma-dhātu of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*).
"Dhātu" has the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*) or "constituent."
First, because each has its own distinct limits;
second, the principle-dharmadhātu (li-fajie).
The realm (dhātu) has the meaning of "nature" (svabhāva).
This is because inexhaustible phenomena share one and the same nature.
Third is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, which possesses the meaning of both the nature-aspect and the phenomenon-aspect;
this is because the nature-aspect is non-obstructive.
Fourth is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena.
All phenomena, defined by their respective boundaries,
are each interfused with their own nature in a manner that is infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
Contemplation (*guan*): When emotions are exhausted and views are eliminated, one becomes darkly unified with the three dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).
Gate (*men*): This text of eight or nine pages constitutes the contemplation based on this [principle].
Briefly, there are three layers, excluding the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
This is because phenomena do not exist independently;
within the fundamental principle of the *dharmadhātu*, no isolated phenomenon exists.
If one contemplates it in isolation,
it is the domain of objective facts and calculations,
rather than the domain of contemplative wisdom.
If analyzed according to its categories, there are four; here,
they are presented in relation to the wisdom that performs the contemplation.
Therefore, there are only three stages.
These three constitute a single path that extends vertically through all levels,
becoming increasingly profound and subtle as one progresses.
There are no second or third [realms] existing separately outside of the initial dharma-realm;
since they do not extend laterally,
it is called "threefold."
Not titled in three sections.
Compiled by the Monk Dushun of Zhongnan Mountain in the Capital. His surname was Du;
his given name was Fashun.
During the early Tang dynasty, he traveled to spread the Dharma;
his divine manifestations were exceedingly numerous,
as evidenced in the biographical records.
It was verified that this was an emanation-body of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
He is the founding patriarch of both the new and old schools of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra;
Venerable Yan is the second patriarch.
The Imperial Preceptor of Kāṅ-tsa (Khangtsang) was the third patriarch;
this was his original composition. According to the principles of the language, it should be stated as "made" (*byas*).
Those who have now gathered like clouds do so because the Patriarch, relying on his own wisdom,
beheld all the Buddhas within the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
All sentient beings—
whether in body and mind,
or in their lands.
Each and every one is the essence and function of this dharma-realm;
such meanings and objects are immeasurable and boundless.
Thereupon, within this immeasurable realm,
he gathered its various categories and organized them into three layers.
I have recorded this directly upon paper for living beings to observe with wisdom;
it is not the same as composing and describing written texts.
Therefore, it is simply called "assemblage" (yǒngjí).
This refers to the meaning of assemblage,
not the assemblage of words.
The first is the ultimate emptiness, which is the dharma-realm of principle.
Examining its fundamental substance,
it is nothing other than the original mind.
Now, because it distinguishes [itself] from false and delusive thoughts,
it is called "True.
Because it distinguishes [itself] from physical obstructions and material forms, [it is called "Formless"].
Therefore, it is called "emptiness.
Second, the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena; this is precisely what is named the Dharma-realm.
Third, the all-pervasive inclusion of phenomena within phenomena, the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena.

The Contemplation of True Emptiness: First, the Method of the Contemplation of True Emptiness briefly opens four phrases and ten gates: (1) the contemplation of returning form to emptiness; (2) the contemplation of clarifying that emptiness is identical to form; (3) the contemplation of the non-obstruction of emptiness and form; and (4) the contemplation of their total cessation and lack of dependence.
Within the first gate, there are four [sections]: the first three distinguish [the nature of] mental afflictions (*kleśa*), while the last one reveals the principle (*tattva*).
Among the first three, one [section] distinguishes [it from] the emptiness of annihilation (*uccheda-śūnyatā*).
The commentary concludes its explanation by stating:
"Because it is real and not annihilated.
This second point distinguishes it from substantial form (*rūpa*).
The commentary concludes its explanation by stating:
"Since the emptiness of non-substantiality is neither blue nor yellow,
it is called 'real form'."
Based on deluded conceptualization, they are reckoned as having a truly existent self-nature;
therefore, one does not distinguish between the provisional and the real by means of the two types of form— shape and color.
According to conventional sentiment, both form and color are considered real;
however, in this passage, color is used as an analogy for shape.
In the text of the third pair of distinctions, it simply states that "form is resolved back into emptiness."
In space there is necessarily no form.
Therefore, according to the underlying meaning, every phrase excludes emotional conceptualization and severs the attachment to emptiness as a substantial form.
According to the literal text, however, the first two phrases are presented through mutual implication by way of ellipsis.
The third point is the "Brief Clarification of the Two.
The *Ratnagotravibhāga* also briefly clarifies the bodhisattva Saṃbhrāntamati’s reckoning of three kinds of emptiness,
fearing that it would burden the wisdom of contemplation.
It is not necessary to harmonize them;
even when harmonized, they are not entirely identical. "A single form is not itself emptiness" is because it is itself emptiness—this is the thesis (*pratijñā*).
For what reason?—this is the inquiry (*praśna*).
The following section provides the explanation;
the final section provides the conclusion.
All other parts should be understood by analogy with these.
"Form is not itself the emptiness of annihilation, and therefore it is not [merely] empty. This explains the preceding phrase.
"Emptiness of annihilation" refers to a void, desolate state of total cessation.
It is not the true mind;
it is without knowledge and without function,
and cannot manifest the myriad dharmas.
This is of two kinds:
namely, the emptiness that is the separation from form and light,
and the emptiness of annihilation.
Regarding "emptiness apart from form":
emptiness exists outside of form,
like a place being non-empty within a wall while the space outside the wall is empty.
Regarding the emptiness of annihilation:
it clarifies emptiness by extinguishing form,
just as digging a well removes earth to reveal space.
It is necessary to extinguish form;
now, to distinguish this [view] from that,
it is said that it is not a void of annihilation.
Therefore, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says:
"To claim that something previously existed and subsequently ceased to exist is nihilism."
However, both the non-Buddhist outsiders and the followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) possess the view of annihilationism.
The annihilationism of the outsiders reverts to the Great Void;
the annihilationism of the two vehicles reverts to Nirvana.
Therefore, the *Zhao lun* states:
"The greatest affliction is none other than having a body;
thus, one extinguishes the body to return to non-being."
"Nothing is more wearying than possessing wisdom;
therefore, sever wisdom to sink into emptiness.
It further says:
Form is a shackle;
wisdom is a mixed poison.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
If the essence of the mind were to perish, it would not differ from the nihilistic conceptual proliferation of the non-Buddhists;
for the entire substance of form is true emptiness. Thus it says, "Because it is identical with emptiness," which explains the subsequent phrase.
Because form and so forth are fundamentally True Suchness (tathatā) and the One Mind,
their conjunction with arising and ceasing is termed the ālayavijñāna and so forth.
It acts as the transformer,
transforming and giving rise to the sense organs, the physical body, and the receptacle world;
these are precisely what are referred to here as the various phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Therefore, when we now investigate it,
it has no substantial body at all;
it returns to the emptiness of the true mind.
It is not appropriate to return to a void of annihilation,
because it is not a transformation of an originally non-existent void.
As for what is meant by "returning":
The text follows below.
This is truly because it is *śūnyatā* (emptiness) as suchness; therefore, it is not a nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*).

This concludes the explanation of what was interpreted. Thus, it is said: "Because this is emptiness-as-suchness, it is not a nihilistic emptiness. This concludes the preceding section, which summarizes the lower clause.
The following connects to the preceding phrase.

Second, form is not identical to emptiness; yet it is identical to emptiness. Why? Because the characteristics of blue and yellow are not the principle of true emptiness; thus it is said they are "not identical to emptiness. This explains the preceding phrase.
Having heard the sutras state that form is empty,
they do not understand that the nature of form is empty;
instead, they grasp at the characteristics of form and take them to be true emptiness.
Therefore, there must be a distinction.
This excludes ordinary beings and bodhisattvas at the initial stage of practice,
but does not exclude those of the Hīnayāna.
The Hinayana does not reckon that form (*rūpa*) is identical to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

However, since blue and yellow have no intrinsic substance and there is nothing that is not entirely empty and non-existent, it is said that they are "identical to emptiness. This explains the latter phrase [of the verse], which clarifies the meaning of "Reality" (*tattva*).
However, while it was previously stated that form (*rūpa*) is in its entirety true emptiness,
it is now said that blue and yellow have no substance and are not without being empty;
although they are called "blue and yellow," [they are nonetheless empty].
This includes length, shortness, and so forth;
for blue, yellow, and other colors necessarily depend upon material obstruction (*sapratigha*).
Thus, space possesses three meanings by which it negates form (*rūpa*).
First, the meaning of being boundless:
if space were finite,
then there would be material phenomena existing outside the realm of space.
Since emptiness has no boundaries,
it encompasses the full extent of the ten directions,
with nothing existing beyond it.
Furthermore, where else could there be phenomena such as form? Regarding the second point,
the meaning of non-destruction,
those who are deluded say:
Although space has no exterior,
why should it prevent form and other phenomena from existing solely within the realm of space? Therefore,
it is refuted by means of the principle of indestructibility.
That is to say, if an object enters into space,
then according to the dimensions and magnitude of that object,
it pierces through space to accommodate it.
Just as a wooden stake driven into the earth,
or a nail or wedge driven into wood,
all penetrate the earth and so forth according to the dimensions of the stake and other such objects.
If the earth and so forth were not subject to disintegration,
then it would not allow a wedge or similar object to enter.
The opponent offers this defense:
Just as water cannot be pierced or broken,
yet allows objects to enter into it,
how could space be any different?
The Refutation says:
Although water is not broken,
when objects enter it, [it is affected].
According to the size and volume of the objects,
arrange them so as to accommodate their contents;
for the nature of water is supremely supple.
It is because [water] is subject to flowing, shifting,
and moving; how could empty space possibly be the same as this water that undergoes movement when pushed aside?
Third is the meaning of non-confusion.
That is to say, some deluded ones further claim that there is no external space-element (ākāśa-dhātu).
The essence of emptiness is indestructible;
it does not obstruct the myriad things that all exist within it,
for emptiness is void, pervasive, and without hindrance.
"Because it is capable of containing.
[The opponent] refutes this, saying:
"If an object were in space..."
Furthermore, emptiness is neither destroyed nor transformed;
its substance would necessarily be indistinguishably mixed with emptiness,
like a single mass of solid and dense matter.
A square pavilion of one foot:
this empty space within the dimensions of the square foot is neither destroyed nor transformed.
If it originally occupies a space of one foot in this direction,
then how could it not be intermingled with the objects occupying that same foot-measure?
If one says they are not mixed,
then one must necessarily be eliminated and the other preserved.
If one says both are preserved yet remain unmixed, [this is untenable].
Then, within the span of one chi,
each would occupy five cun of ground; in this way,
they would successively fail to correspond with one another.
If it is claimed that both exist and pervade a single foot-length [of space],
this is also logically untenable. Why?
Since emptiness and form possess two mutually contradictory characteristics,
they should not occupy the same location as an identical whole.
What are these two contradictions?
The first emptiness is the absence of substance;
form is that which possesses substance.
The second emptiness is voidness and penetration.
Form is characterized by substantial resistance;
it cannot be divided into square inches or fractions,
nor can it be said that it is entirely non-existent.
Furthermore, it is said that they are entirely substantial entities;
yet it cannot be said that they are entirely empty and pervasive;
and again, it is said that they are entirely characterized by material obstruction.
How could such a principle exist?
Therefore, it was stated above that the characteristics of blue and yellow are not the principle of true emptiness.
This means that blue, yellow, and all other colors are without exception empty.
Thus we know that since space is boundless, indestructible, and unmixed,
there can certainly be no color within it.
Therefore, it is said that they "are emptiness.

For the reason that the emptiness which lacks the substance of blue and yellow is not identical to blue and yellow, it is said that they "are not identical to emptiness. This refers to the emptiness that lacks substantiality.
Since the fetters do not possess the characteristic of form,
one clarifies that emptiness is non-existent; how,
then, could there be anything to clarify?

The three colors are not identical to emptiness, yet they are identical to emptiness because within emptiness there is no color; they are not identical to emptiness because when one realizes that color has no substantial essence, it is precisely emptiness. This interpretation is truly because realizing that color returns to emptiness means that within emptiness there is necessarily no color; this is a definitive and decisive conclusion.
The Heart Sūtra of Prajñāpāramitā says:
"Therefore, in emptiness there is no form;
no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
The twelve bases,
the eighteen elements,
and the twelve links of dependent origination.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths and so forth,
the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-sūtra* asks: "What is within this?"
Furthermore, it allows for other things;
therefore, because form is empty and non-existent, form is not the true emptiness. The above constitutes the topical sentences.
The three preceding gates have finished distinguishing phenomena from deluded emotions. This concludes the summary of the three gates.

The four form-aggregates are emptiness. Why is this? Because all phenomena of form are necessarily not different from true emptiness, for all phenomena of form are necessarily devoid of intrinsic nature and exist only through dependence on conditions.
Because the absence of nature in the dependent is itself the perfected nature,
form is emptiness; it is neither the extinction of form nor the preservation of form.
Neither identical nor separate;
therefore, it is identical with true emptiness.
Emptiness is not a form or characteristic of matter.
There is no imagined nature (parikalpita).
The dependent origination (paratantra) is without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva),
and this truth of being without intrinsic nature is precisely the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna).
An ancient said:
"When form departs, emptiness does not remain;
emptiness does not abide within limits."
Reflect on this: just as it is with the emptiness of form, so it is with all phenomena. Form is the foremost of the characteristics of phenomena and the first of the five aggregates;
therefore, whenever the various sūtras wish to explain the meaning of emptiness, [they begin with form].
All of these are explained in terms of form (*rūpa*).
For instance, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* enumerates more than eighty categories and names;
all of these are treated as examples of form.
To show the essential point:
it encompasses the sentient beings of the six realms,
as well as the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and followers of the Two Vehicles throughout the ten directions.
These are the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.
Since this school maintains that defilement and purity are non-dual in their characteristics,
one should say that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not themselves annihilation-emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*).
The patterns of blue, yellow,
and so forth are what are termed the aspects of apprehension and so on;
they are not the principle of true emptiness.
This extends even to the Buddhas.
To say that such things as the marks of supernatural powers and radiance are not the principle of true emptiness is precisely why the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical characteristics.
The second section, clarifying the contemplation that emptiness is identical to form, also contains four gates— distinguishing delusion to reveal understanding,
the heading, the inquiry, the explanation, and the conclusion—
each as previously described.
The four gates merely involve a reversal of the textual momentum to establish the subsequent passage on the non-obstruction of emptiness and form,
wherein all distinctions are extinguished and there is no place for dependence.
Regarding the passage in the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* beginning with "emptiness is form" and so forth,
only the third clause is not a case of reciprocal opposition.
The meaning is likewise not different.
Each point, taken in reverse order from above, establishes the Middle Way; there is no further distinct meaning.

"First, emptiness is not identical to form" is because emptiness is identical to form. Why? Because a nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*) is not identical to form; thus it is said, "it is not form. This explains the preceding phrase.
"Because true emptiness is necessarily not different from form, it is said that 'emptiness is itself form. This explains the latter phrase.
"It must be through true emptiness being identical to form... This concludes the latter phrase.
"...therefore, [the view of] empty space as a mere negation does not identify with form. This concludes the former phrase.

The two kinds of emptiness do not coincide with form, because emptiness is identical to form. Why is this? Because the principle of emptiness is neither blue nor yellow; thus it is said they do not coincide with form. This explains the preceding phrase.
"However, because it is not different from blue and yellow, one says that emptiness is form. This explains the latter phrase.
"It is precisely because it is not different from blue and yellow that it is not identical to blue and yellow. This is the concluding explanation.
Therefore it is said: "Form is not identical to form. This concludes the heading.

Regarding the three emptinesses, they are not identical to form because emptiness is identical to form. Why is this? Because emptiness is that which is relied upon (*āśraya*), not that which relies; therefore, it is not identical to form. This explains the preceding phrase.
Regarding the formlessness in the space above:
formlessness is precisely that upon which form depends,
just as there is no shadow within the brightness of a mirror.
"Because it necessarily serves as the support for that which depends upon it, it is itself form (*rūpa*). This explains the latter clause.
Because it is formless, it can serve as the support for form, like the clarity within a mirror.
Because it is devoid of an image,
it is able to serve as the basis for an image; therefore,
it is not identical to the image itself.
This is not a counter-argument that contradicts the preceding text;
for within emptiness there is no form,
which is supported by both principle and scriptural authority.
Within form there is no emptiness;
both principle and phenomena are utterly transcended.
Therefore, the distinction is made solely by way of the relationship between the supporting and the supported.
As for the principle:
within a maṇi jewel,
colors such as black and so forth must necessarily not exist.
Regarding those with scriptural evidence,
it is as cited above;
the Sūtra says:
Therefore, within emptiness there is no form,
and no sensation, perception, and so forth.
As for the phrase "the principle is severed":
Regarding the colors manifested by the jewel:
wherever there is color, there must necessarily be a bright pearl.
As for "the excellence of the pattern":
In all the holy teachings, nowhere is there a passage stating that emptiness does not exist within form.
This is because it is the basis [of form]; yet, because it is not identical to the basis, it is not itself form. To explain this conclusion: therefore, by virtue of not being identical to form...
"Therefore, it is precisely form (*rūpa*). This concludes the summary by way of its meaning.
The three preceding sections have also finished using phenomena (*dharma*) to distinguish them from emotional attachments.

Why is it that the four emptinesses (*catasraḥ śūnyatāḥ*) are themselves form? Because whatever is true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*) is necessarily not different from form; for this is the principle of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), which is the very essence of true emptiness.
This refers to the True Suchness (tathatā) manifested by the two kinds of emptiness.
Because it is not a state of annihilation, True Suchness does not abide in its own nature.
The preceding [sections] have all been explained.
Therefore, emptiness is itself form—this is the summary.
Just as it is with emptiness and form, so it is with all phenomena; reflect upon this. Since true emptiness is not different from form, [it is identical].
Nor is it different from all phenomena,
as illustrated previously. Third.
The Contemplation of the Non-obstruction between Emptiness and Form: Although the two characters "emptiness" (kōng) and "form" (sè) appear,
the fundamental intent resides solely in emptiness,
for form is but a hollow name and a hollow appearance.
It possesses not even a hair’s breadth of substantial form;
therefore, those who cultivate this contemplation do so with their minds directed toward this very point.
In the text, when taking form as the primary subject, it says "emptiness appears";
when taking emptiness as the primary subject, it does not say "form appears," yet it still states that "emptiness is not concealed."
Therefore, it is called only the "Contemplation of True Emptiness" (zhēnkōng guān) and not the "Contemplation of True Emptiness and Delusory Form.

This means that because form in its entirety is no different from emptiness—it is the very emptiness that exhausts all form—when form is exhausted, emptiness manifests. Because emptiness in its entirety is no different from form—it is the very form that exhausts all emptiness—emptiness is itself form, and thus emptiness is not concealed. This is the textual passage concerning form and emptiness.
Each section consists of two phrases:
the first indicates the reason for being unimpeded,
while the latter sets forth the characteristics of that unimpedement.
That is to say, if form were substantial form,
it would obstruct space;
space would then be a mere void of annihilation.
That which obstructs is form;
since form is now illusory form,
it does not obstruct space.
Emptiness is true emptiness;
therefore, it does not obstruct form.
An alternative version of the text says:
It is also consistent that emptiness manifests while form is not yet exhausted;
however, it is not as [effective] as non-existence.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva contemplates form, there is nothing that is not seen as emptiness; contemplating emptiness, there is nothing that is not seen as form. Being without obstruction or hindrance, it is a dharma of a single flavor (*ekarasa*), which can be perceived through reflection.
Fourth, the Contemplation of Utter Extinction and Non-Reliance. This section has two parts.
First, this contemplation is explained;
subsequently, the four gates are comprehensively distinguished.
Within the first [section], there are two parts.
First, there is the complete cessation;
second, the investigation and explanation of the reason for it.
Regarding the first, the text says "it cannot be," and so forth.
Since the original text itself provides its own explanation,
there is no need for me to annotate it here.
Furthermore, the subsequent textual passages develop in various ways.
Now, I shall briefly provide a separate explanation by correlating it with the text below.
That is to say, this emptiness of true reality (śūnyatā) which is being contemplated cannot be said to be identical to form (*rūpa*).
If emptiness were identical to form, then the noble ones (*ārya*) would have to see false form just as ordinary people do.
If one were to correspond with the holy ones by perceiving true emptiness, there would likewise be no two truths.
If it were not identical to form, then one would perceive emptiness as existing outside of form.
There would be no way for noble wisdom to be accomplished;
furthermore, ordinary beings and sages would be eternally separate,
because the sage would not be attained from the ordinary being.
The first two lines refute the preceding second contemplation.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that form is identical to emptiness; for if form were identical to emptiness...
If those who are deluded perceive forms,
they should— just like the noble wisdom— perceive them as empty;
otherwise, they will also lose sight of the two truths.
If it were not identical with emptiness,
then ordinary beings would not be deluded when perceiving form;
furthermore, regarding the form perceived by ordinary beings:
"Long separated from true emptiness,
one will certainly not become a sage.
These two lines refute the initial contemplation mentioned previously.
"All dharmas are likewise ungraspable. This concludes the preceding analogy.
As stated above: "If it is so for the emptiness of form, so it is for all dharmas."
It is so. "Neither can" and "also cannot"— seeing that all these are "cannot" is likewise a conceptual discrimination.
These words are also not accepted; acceptance itself is conceptualization.
Utterly severed and without dependence, Prajñā manifests before one.
It is beyond the reach of speech; the path of language is cut off.
It is not reached by understanding, because the sphere of mental activity has ceased and it cannot be known by cognition.
This is called the sphere of practice; there are two spheres:
first, the sphere of practice.
Now, the mind merges with the object; merging the mind,
one leaves behind discursive wisdom,
only then arriving at this state.
It is clarified that only practice can reach [the goal],
for it is not through understanding the object.
Second, such is their dark harmony.
This is precisely true practice.
Practice is itself the object,
because it is the delimitation of practice.

Why is this? Because as soon as the mind arises or a thought moves, one immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma and loses right mindfulness. This is the second [section], which interrogates and then explains.
The principle of true emptiness is inherently and naturally so.
However, because one is deluded by it—
stirring thoughts and clinging to signs—
it is necessary to investigate and dismantle them, thereby discerning emotion and revealing principle.
Now that emotions have been forgotten and wisdom has vanished,
there is only the original reality;
what need is there for the numerical calculations of newly arisen understanding?
If there is any conceptualization of numbers,
this constitutes the stirring of thought;
the stirring of thought gives rise to the mind.
Therefore, one loses right mindfulness.
As for right mindfulness,
it is knowing through non-thought.
If there were no cognition at all, what could be called right mindfulness?
Below this, the four gates are collectively distinguished.
Furthermore, regarding the first two lines of the preceding four lines, all eight gates exclude emotional afflictions (*kleśa*), each consisting of the first three phrases.
The "Manifestation of Understanding" (khyen-pa) corresponds to each final phrase.

The third phrase concludes the understanding of a single gateway and leads toward practice; the fourth phrase constitutes the actual essence of the practice of a single gateway. The above is the analysis of the correct practice.
The following section serves as a counter-illustration to show their mutual dependence,
like the way the eyes and feet further assist one another.
Furthermore, the first phrase brings form back to emptiness.
There is no superimposition;
secondly, clarifying that emptiness is identical to form,
there is no denial.
The three emptinesses and form are unimpeded;
this is not a state of double negation,
free from the slanders of conceptual proliferation.
The four are utterly extinguished and have no locus of dependence;
they are neither "both empty and form" nor subject to the contradiction of mutual denial.
The four types of slander being absent,
the hundredfold negations are severed;
this corresponds to the eight sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
This is the ultimate pinnacle of the signless Mahāyāna;
how much more so the latter two contemplations, which become increasingly profound and mysterious.
Furthermore, the first phrase indicates that form is itself emptiness.
The second phrase corresponds to "emptiness is itself form.
The third corresponds to "form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form.

it is also like a mustard seed in a jar;
it is also like pure gold.
When manifesting as the forms of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, and sentient beings of the six realms,
they appear simultaneously with all these images,
without the slightest concealment.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of anything that does not correspond.
Now, the rational nature is likewise;
there is not even a hair’s breadth of concealment.
Furthermore, there is not even a hair’s breadth of activity;
this is not the same as the contemplation of true emptiness,
nor the gate of subsuming phenomena by principle.
This is simply the manifestation of principle.
Therefore, it is said next:
"In this case, phenomena have no separate reality; rather, the entirety of principle constitutes phenomena. This is the preceding explanation.
The following passage uses human experience as proof:

"Therefore, although a bodhisattva contemplates phenomena, this very contemplation is the contemplation of principle; yet, it is said that these phenomena do not coincide with principle, because they do not destroy the phenomena."
Regarding the two matters as they accord with reality:
each individual matter is, in accordance with reality, pervasive and vast;
in accordance with reality, it penetrates the three periods of time.
It abides eternally as it truly is;

that is to say, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are not different from the principle (*tattva*). This is because they have previously emerged from pervasiveness, and by virtue of the principle of the preceding gate, they are identical to phenomena.
Phenomena do not differ from principle;
therefore, this [section] and the preceding section mutually correspond as a pair.
Furthermore, it relates to the subsequent section by being neither identical nor different when viewed in relation to one another.
"Being able to pervade and being able to contain" form a pair;
thus, phenomena follow principle to achieve perfect pervasion—this is the general statement of the thesis.

Below, the specific characteristics of pervasion are demonstrated: it causes even a single atom to be universally pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and when the entire body of the Dharma-realm pervades all phenomena, this single atom likewise exists entirely within all phenomena in accordance with its rational nature. This is explained by taking a single phenomenon as an illustrative example.

Just as it is with a single atom, so it is with all phenomena; this applies by analogy to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and sentient beings of the six realms—one by one, they are all thus.
Section Three: The Door of the Three Matters Encompassing Both Principle and Phenomena. This section has two parts:
first, the direct explanation of this door;
second, the general synthesis of the two doors.

This means that because all phenomena (*dharmas*) and their underlying principles are not identical, a single fundamental phenomenon can extensively accommodate them while maintaining its own identity. It is like a single minute atom: although its form is not large, it can contain and encompass the boundless *dharmadhātu*. Since lands and all other phenomena are not separate from the *dharmadhātu*, they all manifest together within a single atom. This points to one thing as an illustration.
Because the preceding point encompasses the principle,
all other points are likewise included.
Because its essence is not different from the principles it contains,
it manifests all those contained principles within a single phenomenon.
However, this is not different from the principle that [the container] must be capable of containing; here,

Because the single matter of "preserving the source" (*yuan-cun-ben*) functions as the containing reality (*neng-han-fa*), and furthermore because it is contrasted with the preceding category;

just as one atom [contains all phenomena], so too do all phenomena—this is the established analogy. Since this principle and these phenomena are mutually pervasive, being neither identical nor different, there are four propositions in total. This constitutes the aspect of being the "containing limit."
All of them fully possess the meaning of being neither identical to nor different from the principle (*tattva*).
Because they are not identical, their substantial existence (*sabhāva*) serves as that which contains [the principle].

This means that because all phenomena (*dharmas*) and their underlying principle are neither identical nor distinct, they are both particularized and universal. Consequently, these phenomena do not depart from a single location, yet they entirely pervade within every atom throughout the ten directions. Because they are not distinct, they are not one; thus, while they entirely pervade the ten directions, they do not move from a single position. They are simultaneously distant and near, simultaneously pervasive and stationary, unobstructed and unhindered.
Section Five: The Gate of Unimpeded Broadness and Narrowness. This explains the third gate.

It means that because phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*) are not identical, [the atom] is narrow; yet because they are not different, it is broad. Without destroying a single atom, it can extensively contain the ocean of lands of the ten directions; because it is not different, it is not identical. Thus, while it extensively contains the dharma-realm of the ten directions, the minute atom does not increase in size. Therefore, the phenomenon of a single atom is simultaneously broad and narrow, simultaneously great and small, without obstruction or impediment.
The sixth is the gate of universal non-obstruction;
the sixth and seventh gates both combine the preceding fourth and fifth,
while also incorporating the second and third.
Because they are extensive, inclusive, pervasive, and inseparable:
two and four are exclusively pervasive;
three and five are exclusively inclusive.
Therefore, they are now combined;
both are present simultaneously,
differing only in that the one and the many are viewed in reciprocal relation to one another.
Thus, two gates—the sixth and the seventh—are established.
Within the text, there are two pairs.
The first clarifies that pervasion is itself inclusion.
The latter clarifies that "accommodating" (*yō*) is identical to "pervasive" (*hen*).
Regarding the first point, it says:

"That is to say, when this single atom is considered in relation to all [atoms], by virtue of its universal pervasion, it is 'broadly accommodating' (*kōyō*); for it takes one and looks toward the many."
Therefore, there is the sense of universal inclusion;
for since those many [phenomena] can each be universally encompassed,
they can all be fully contained.
If many were expected from one,
this principle would not hold,
because that which is expected is only one.
One cannot say that it pervades all speech;

Therefore, when it is omnipresent within all things, it simultaneously withdraws all phenomena back into itself and abides entirely within its own self;

If one uses the analogy of mirrors and lamps:
suppose eight mirrors are arranged in the four cardinal and four intermediate directions,
with one mirror placed above and one below, making ten in total.
Within that, place a single lamp;

When a single mirror pervades the other nine mirrors, [the same occurs for all].
This means that nine [atoms] are contained within one.

Furthermore, because this capacity to contain extensively is itself all-pervasive, it causes this single atom to likewise pervade all the distinct phenomena within its own interior. However, when one contains nine, it merely covers the upper portion.

Therefore, when this object-particle itself pervades another, that other simultaneously pervades it; one should contemplate how they can contain and enter one another, being simultaneously and universally encompassed without obstruction.

yet resides within my capacity to enter many;

Immediately, that single mirror is withdrawn and returns within the nine mirrors of the "entering" [state],

yet it causes all things to be capable of entering it.
Constantly abiding within one, that one is the object of entry.
Simultaneously contemplate them without obstruction: this means that when each of the nine is individually contained within itself,

That is to say, when considering a single dharma in relation to all that exists, there are four permutations regarding its inclusion within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). That is, many [subjects] looking toward one [object].

each of these is paired with four propositions.
As for that which is encompassed:
Each individual dharma is subsumed within one [of the] bases (āyatana) and one [of the] elements (dhātu).
This is the third phrase among the eight;

Third: one dharma encompasses one and includes all;

This is the first complete phrase among the eight;
it is combined with the fourth phrase among the nine.
Next, all phenomena are taken as that which performs the inclusion.
Regarding each of these being subsumed within the four propositions:
first, all phenomena are entirely subsumed within one single basis;
this is the complete affirmative proposition among the eight.
This corresponds to the first phrase among the nine.
Second, "all dharmas are subsumed within all, and each enters into one";
this is the first half of the final phrase among the eight.
The second half of the subsequent line corresponds with the second line of the ninefold [classification]. Third,
all phenomena are subsumed within one, and one is subsumed within all.
This consists of the first half of the second verse among the eight,
and the second half of the final verse;

The fourth [point] is that all phenomena are subsumed within, and enter into, all [phenomena].

which is combined with the final phrase of the ninth [section].
When these two gates are thus interwoven and assigned to one another,
they unfold in infinite layers,
and the gate of the mutual fusion of the principal and its attendants opens wide.
By universally applying these ten gates to all phenomena and meanings,
one then fully realizes the principle of the Ten Mysterious Gates.
If one merely pairs these ten with the Ten Profundities,
the textual structure becomes disjointed. Rather,
one should cause them to appear clearly and perfectly, so that they accord with the sphere of practice— unobstructed and unimpeded— and through deep contemplation, bring them into manifest presence.
The Commentary on the *Huayan fajie guanmen* concludes.
